conventions.convention: Exact estimability means a single fixed probe gives an unbiased linear estimator for every x in X; membership in the closure of the adjoint range does not suffice.

The Gaussian model uses separable real Hilbert spaces, positive noise level, and an injective positive self-adjoint trace-class prior covariance. The posterior theorem assumes AC and supplied complete orthonormal bases, including finite and empty bases.
Data are fields on H equipped with the cylinder sigma-algebra. The posterior mean identity holds almost surely for each fixed feature; its exceptional set may depend on the feature.
The raw test rejects by the strict comparison y(Φ_h)>c_h and is defined for every field input, including inputs outside the prior-predictive probability-one set.

The calibrated level bound applies to x=i(v) with norm of v at most one and feature at most zero. The zero-probe calibrated test never rejects. The weighted minimizer identity additionally requires C0 to commute with K*K.
Level one means the supremum of rejection probabilities over the unrestricted null half-space is one; attainment at a finite parameter is not asserted.

load_bearing.statement: Under the stated Gaussian model, AC and supplied-basis hypotheses, a data-indexed posterior kernel exists and is Gaussian with mean M_y and covariance ε²SRS for every y. For each fixed h, its mean satisfies ⟨M_y,h⟩=⟨m0,h⟩+y(Φ_h)−⟨Km0,Φ_h⟩ for P_Y-almost every y.

The raw test has the stated Gaussian rejection probability, with a separate zero-probe branch, and agrees almost surely under the prior-predictive law with positivity of the posterior marginal mode. The calibrated probe test has level at most α on the stated null ball. Under C0K*K=K*KC0, Φ_h minimizes the stated extended-valued weighted functional and K*Φ_h=B(B+ε²I)⁻¹h.
A continuous linear feature is exactly linearly estimable by one probe precisely when its Riesz vector belongs to R(K*); every such probe has variance ε² times its squared H-norm.
Under the stated Gaussian model, if C0K*K=K*KC0, h≠0, and Bh is not a scalar multiple of h, then the supremum of raw-test rejection probabilities over {x:⟨x,h⟩≤0} equals one.

concerns.concern: Proof 5.1 concludes that each field evaluation is measurable with respect to the completion of G=σ(Y(e_n):n), and hence that the full field sigma-algebra is contained in that completion. Almost-sure equality with a G-measurable variable only gives this for the ambient augmentation by all ambient null events; it need not give membership in the ordinary completion of G. For example, take X=H=R, K=0, ε=1, an independent standard-normal prior U, standard-normal ξ and an independent Bernoulli(0) coordinate with event N={coordinate=1}. Set Z(g)=gξ except Z(2)=2ξ+1_N. This satisfies the stated Gaussian and L2-linearity assumptions. With supplied basis {1}, G=σ(ξ), while the full field reveals N through Y(2)−2Y(1). N is not contained in any G-measurable null set. The theorem's independence conclusion remains accessible directly from the already established independence with every finite observation block and a generating-cylinder argument, but the written completion inclusion needs qualification.

Proof 1.1 writes the intermediate tail expression as '1-G((c-⟨x,K*Φ⟩)/(ε‖Φ‖)' in its LaTeX formula: the outer G parenthesis is unclosed. The statement's displayed probability formula and the subsequent calculation are correct.

seams_checked.note: The owned items use the supplier's isonormal field experiment, cylinder sigma-algebra, L2 linearity and probe covariance. They preserve real-space and positive-noise hypotheses and do not treat white noise as an H-valued observation.

The compact-model prerequisite is used by the examples with compactness proved explicitly. Exact estimability is characterized by the actual adjoint range, not its closure. No closed-range or bounded-pseudoinverse conclusion is imported into the general bounded-forward-map tests.

The design page lists the owned page as a prerequisite. Its listed items contain no direct citation to the owned items. The finite Gaussian information-gain theorem instead cites its separate finite posterior supplier, explicitly allowing singular prior covariance; it does not attribute that extension to the owned injective-covariance posterior theorem.
